content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
10	  `loop` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
30	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
31	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
32	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
33	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
34	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
35	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
36	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
37	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
38	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
39	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
40	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
41	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
42	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
43	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
44	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
45	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
46	  set (delivery is at least once);
47	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
48	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
49	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
50	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
51	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
52	
53	## Requirements
54	
55	- Python 3.11 or newer
56	- no third-party runtime dependencies
57	
58	## Run the service
59	
60	```bash
61	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
62	```
63	
64	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
65	has bound the port.
66	
67	## HTTP API
68	
69	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
70	
71	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
72	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
73	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
74	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
75	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
76	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
77	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
78	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
79	
80	### Tenants and quotas
81	
82	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
83	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
84	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
85	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
86	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
87	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
88	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
89	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
90	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
91	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
92	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
93	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
94	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
95	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
96	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
97	
98	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
99	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
100	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, queue pulls, acknowledgements,
101	and all history and status queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics
102	queries. An empty
103	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
104	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
105	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
106	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
107	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
108	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
109	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
110	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
111	the usual `409 conflict`.
112	
113	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
114	hold:
115	
116	```http
117	PUT /quotas
118	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
119	X-Tenant-Id: acme
120	
121	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
122	```
123	
124	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
125	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
126	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
127	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
128	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
129	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
130	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
131	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
132	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
133	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
134	
135	```http
136	GET /quotas
137	X-Tenant-Id: acme
138	```
139	
140	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
141	when the tenant has declared none.
142	
143	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
144	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
145	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
146	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
147	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
148	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
149	
150	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
151	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
152	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
153	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
154	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
155	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
156	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
157	
158	### Usage metering and billing
159	
160	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
161	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
162	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
163	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
164	metered action types are:
165	
166	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
167	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
168	  definition;
169	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
170	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
171	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
172	  `schedule_triggered`;
173	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
174	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
175	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
176	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
177	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
178	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
179	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
180	  meters nothing.
181	
182	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
183	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
184	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
185	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
186	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
187	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
188	
189	```http
190	GET /usage
191	X-Tenant-Id: acme
192	```
193	
194	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
195	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
196	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
197	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
198	
199	```http
200	GET /bill
201	X-Tenant-Id: acme
202	```
203	
204	Returns the per-type bill:
205	
206	```json
207	{"bill":{"items":[
208	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
209	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
210	],"total":2100}}
211	```
212	
213	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
214	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
215	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
216	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
217	
218	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
219	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`. Usage and bill data follow the
220	usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see another's records.
221	
222	### Operational metrics
223	
224	```http
225	GET /metrics
226	X-Tenant-Id: acme
227	```
228	
229	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
230	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
231	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
232	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
233	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
234	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
235	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
236	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
237	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
238	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
239	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
240	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
241	
242	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
243	timestamp ending in `Z`:
244	
245	```http
246	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
247	X-Tenant-Id: acme
248	```
249	
250	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
251	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
252	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
253	  counts every recorded fact;
254	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
255	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
256	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
257	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
258	  result.
259	
260	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
261	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
262	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
263	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
264	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
265	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
266	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
267	completion or termination event.
268	
269	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
270	
271	```http
272	GET /metrics/export
273	X-Tenant-Id: acme
274	```
275	
276	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
277	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
278	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
279	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
280	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
281	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
282	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
283	
284	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
285	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
286	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
287	ordered by ascending label value:
288	
289	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
290	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
291	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
292	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
293	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
294	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
295	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
296	  unlabeled scalar samples.
297	
298	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
299	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
300	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
301	ends with a single newline.
302	
303	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
304	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
305	failures, and schedule triggers:
306	
307	```json
308	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
309	```
310	
311	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
312	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
313	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
314	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
315	  ended for that reason.
316	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
317	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
318	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
319	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
320	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
321	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
322	  another attempt, per node identifier.
323	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
324	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
325	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
326	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
327	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
328	
329	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
330	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
331	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
332	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
333	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
334	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
335	
336	### Health
337	
338	```http
339	GET /health
340	```
341	
342	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
343	
344	### Create a workflow
345	
346	```http
347	POST /workflows
348	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
349	
350	{
351	  "id": "order-flow",
352	  "nodes": [
353	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
354	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
355	  ]
356	}
357	```
358	
359	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
360	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
361	
362	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
363	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
364	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
365	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
366	
367	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
368	
369	```json
370	{
371	  "id": "order-flow",
372	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
373	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
374	}
375	```
376	
377	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
378	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
379	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
380	
381	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
382	
383	```json
384	{
385	  "id": "nightly-orders",
386	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
387	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
388	}
389	```
390	
391	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
392	
393	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
394	
395	```json
396	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
397	```
398	
399	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
400	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
401	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
402	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
403	`false`.
404	
405	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
406	
407	```json
408	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
409	```
410	
411	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
412	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
413	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
414	dependencies of its successors.
415	
416	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
417	
418	```json
419	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
420	```
421	
422	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
423	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
424	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
425	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
426	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
427	`retries_exhausted`.
428	
429	A task may instead declare an approval point:
430	
431	```json
432	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
433	```
434	
435	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
436	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
437	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
438	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
439	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
440	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
441	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
442	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
443	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
444	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
445	move the task.
446	
447	### Submit an approval decision
448	
449	```http
450	POST /executions/run-1/decision
451	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
452	
453	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
454	```
455	
456	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
457	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
458	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
459	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
460	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
461	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
462	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
463	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
464	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
465	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
466	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
467	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
468	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
469	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
470	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
471	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
472	404.
473	
474	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
475	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
476	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
477	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
478	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
479	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
480	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
481	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
482	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
483	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
484	shape and event stream.
485	
486	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
487	segment:
488	
489	```json
490	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
491	```
492	
493	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
494	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
495	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
496	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
497	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
498	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
499	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
500	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
501	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
502	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
503	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
504	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
505	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
506	loop node instead).
507	
508	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
509	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
510	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
511	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
512	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
513	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
514	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
515	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
516	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
517	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
518	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
519	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
520	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
521	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
522	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
523	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
524	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
525	belong only to their iterations.
526	
527	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
528	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
529	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
530	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
531	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
532	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
533	exactly.
534	
535	### Workflow versions
536	
537	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
538	
539	```json
540	{
541	  "id": "order-flow",
542	  "version": "2026-09-25",
543	  "nodes": [
544	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
545	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
546	  ]
547	}
548	```
549	
550	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
551	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
552	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
553	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
554	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
555	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
556	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
557	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
558	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
559	
560	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
561	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
562	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
563	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
564	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
565	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
566	
567	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
568	current version at the moment it starts:
569	
570	```http
571	POST /executions
572	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
573	
574	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
575	```
576	
577	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
578	
579	```json
580	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
581	```
582	
583	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
584	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
585	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
586	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
587	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
588	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
589	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
590	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
591	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
592	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
593	conclusions never change.
594	
595	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
596	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
597	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
598	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
599	stream with no added field.
600	
601	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
602	
603	```http
604	GET /workflows/order-flow
605	```
606	
607	```json
608	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
609	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
610	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
611	]}
612	```
613	
614	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
615	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
616	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
617	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
618	resources as usual.
619	
620	### Migrate a running execution to another version
621	
622	```http
623	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
624	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
625	
626	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
627	```
628	
629	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
630	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
631	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
632	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
633	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
634	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
635	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
636	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
637	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
638	carries the target version.
639	
640	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
641	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
642	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
643	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
644	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
645	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
646	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
647	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
648	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
649	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
650	
651	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
652	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
653	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
654	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
655	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
656	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
657	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
658	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
659	content.
660	
661	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
662	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
663	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
664	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
665	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
666	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
667	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
668	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
669	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
670	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
671	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
672	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
673	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
674	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
675	
676	### Start an execution
677	
678	```http
679	POST /executions
680	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
681	
682	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
683	```
684	
685	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
686	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
687	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
688	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
689	
690	An execution may declare a timeout:
691	
692	```json
693	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
694	```
695	
696	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
697	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
698	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
699	a timeout never expire.
700	
701	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
702	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
703	
704	```json
705	{
706	  "id": "run-3",
707	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
708	  "input": {},
709	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
710	}
711	```
712	
713	### Inspect an execution
714	
715	```http
716	GET /executions/run-1
717	GET /executions/run-1/events
718	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
719	```
720	
721	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
722	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
723	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
724	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
725	
726	### Webhook notifications
727	
728	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
729	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
730	
731	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
732	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
733	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
734	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
735	  reason);
736	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
737	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
738	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
739	
740	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
741	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
742	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
743	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
744	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
745	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
746	subscriptions" below.
747	
748	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
749	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
750	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
751	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
752	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
753	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
754	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
755	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
756	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
757	triggered it.
758	
759	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
760	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
761	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
762	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
763	results as before.
764	
765	### Inspect the delivery history
766	
767	```http
768	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
769	```
770	
771	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
772	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
773	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
774	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
775	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
776	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
777	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
778	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
779	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
780	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
781	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
782	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
783	
784	### Queue subscriptions
785	
786	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
787	
788	```json
789	{
790	  "id": "run-4",
791	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
792	  "input": {},
793	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
794	}
795	```
796	
797	A queue subscription contains exactly:
798	
799	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of at most 100 characters;
800	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
801	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
802	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
803	
804	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
805	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
806	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
807	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
808	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
809	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
810	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
811	
812	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
813	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
814	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
815	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
816	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
817	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
818	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
819	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
820	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
821	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
822	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
823	before.
824	
825	### Inspect the queue state
826	
827	```http
828	GET /executions/run-4/queues
829	X-Tenant-Id: acme
830	```
831	
832	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
833	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
834	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
835	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
836	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
837	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
838	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
839	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
840	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
841	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
842	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
843	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
844	
845	### Pull messages from a queue
846	
847	```http
848	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
849	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
850	X-Tenant-Id: acme
851	
852	{}
853	```
854	
855	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
856	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
857	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
858	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
859	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
860	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
861	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
862	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
863	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
864	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
865	
866	### Acknowledge a message
867	
868	```http
869	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/ack
870	Idempotency-Key: ack-request-1
871	X-Tenant-Id: acme
872	
873	{"idempotency_key": "run-4:2:queue:order-events"}
874	```
875	
876	The body must contain exactly `idempotency_key`, naming a message of the
877	queue. Acknowledgement is explicit and final: the message permanently leaves
878	the queue and is never delivered again, and the response is
879	`{"acknowledged": true}`. Acknowledging a message that was already
880	acknowledged, or a key the queue does not know, is a 404 `not_found`.
881	Pulling from or acknowledging a queue the execution does not have, or one
882	belonging to a missing or cross-tenant execution, is likewise a 404
883	`not_found`. Pull and acknowledge are idempotent commands like every other
884	operation: repeating one with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the
885	original result, and reusing a key across different operations is a 409
886	`conflict`.
887	
888	### Schedules
889	
890	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
891	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
892	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
893	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
894	
895	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
896	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
897	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
898	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
899	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
900	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
901	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
902	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
903	
904	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
905	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
906	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
907	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
908	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
909	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
910	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
911	created is exposed through the status query below.
912	
913	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
914	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
915	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
916	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
917	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
918	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
919	
920	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
921	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
922	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
923	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
924	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
925	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
926	
927	### Declare or replace a schedule
928	
929	```http
930	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
931	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
932	
933	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
934	```
935	
936	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
937	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
938	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
939	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
940	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
941	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
942	
943	### Inspect the schedule status
944	
945	```http
946	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
947	```
948	
949	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
950	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
951	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
952	
953	```json
954	{
955	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
956	  "paused": false,
957	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
958	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
959	}
960	```
961	
962	The fields are:
963	
964	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
965	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
966	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
967	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
968	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
969	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
970	  `null` until the first period fires;
971	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
972	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
973	
974	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
975	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
976	
977	### Pause and resume a schedule
978	
979	```http
980	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
981	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
982	
983	{}
984	```
985	
986	```http
987	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
988	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
989	
990	{}
991	```
992	
993	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
994	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
995	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
996	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
997	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
998	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
999	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
1000	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
1001	
1002	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
1003	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
1004	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
1005	
1006	### Checkpoints
1007	
1008	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
1009	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
1010	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
1011	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
1012	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
1013	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
1014	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
1015	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
1016	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
1017	duplicating any node output.
1018	
1019	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
1020	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
1021	same state shape and event stream as before.
1022	
1023	### Complete the next ready node
1024	
1025	```http
1026	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1027	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
1028	
1029	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
1030	```
1031	
1032	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
1033	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
1034	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
1035	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
1036	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
1037	the status becomes `completed`.
1038	
1039	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
1040	
1041	```http
1042	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1043	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
1044	
1045	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
1046	```
1047	
1048	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
1049	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
1050	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
1051	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
1052	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
1053	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
1054	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
1055	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
1056	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
1057	
1058	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
1059	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
1060	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
1061	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
1062	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
1063	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
1064	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
1065	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
1066	the execution stream.
1067	
1068	### Cancel an execution
1069	
1070	```http
1071	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
1072	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
1073	```
1074	
1075	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
1076	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
1077	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
1078	
1079	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
1080	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
1081	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
1082	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
1083	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
1084	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
1085	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
1086	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
1087	
1088	### Claim a work item
1089	
1090	```http
1091	POST /executions/run-1/claim
1092	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
1093	
1094	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
1095	```
1096	
1097	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
1098	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
1099	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
1100	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
1101	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
1102	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
1103	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
1104	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
1105	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
1106	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
1107	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
1108	
1109	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
1110	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
1111	
1112	```http
1113	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1114	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
1115	
1116	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1117	```
1118	
1119	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
1120	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
1121	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
1122	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
1123	an execution without any claim.
1124	
1125	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
1126	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
1127	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
1128	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
1129	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
1130	
1131	### Renew a lease
1132	
1133	```http
1134	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
1135	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
1136	
1137	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1138	```
1139	
1140	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
1141	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
1142	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
1143	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
1144	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
1145	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
1146	
1147	### Release a work item
1148	
1149	```http
1150	POST /executions/run-1/release
1151	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
1152	
1153	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1154	```
1155	
1156	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
1157	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
1158	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
1159	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
1160	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
1161	`not_found`.
1162	
1163	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
1164	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
1165	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
1166	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
1167	restarts.
1168	
1169	### Recover from a checkpoint
1170	
1171	```http
1172	POST /executions/run-1/recover
1173	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
1174	
1175	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
1176	```
1177	
1178	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
1179	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
1180	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
1181	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
1182	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
1183	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
1184	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
1185	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
1186	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
1187	execution state and events.
1188	
1189	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
1190	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
1191	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
1192	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
1193	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
1194	stays consistent with the materialized state.
1195	
1196	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
1197	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
1198	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
1199	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
1200	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
1201	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
1202	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
1203	
1204	### Replay
1205	
1206	```http
1207	POST /executions/run-1/replay
1208	```
1209	
1210	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
1211	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
1212	and the rebuilt execution.
1213	
1214	## Errors
1215	
1216	Errors use this shape:
1217	
1218	```json
1219	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
1220	```
1221	
1222	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
1223	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
1224	declarations and the usage, bill, and metrics queries require a tenant, and
1225	quota limits are positive integers validated by the
1226	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
1227	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
1228	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
1229	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
1230	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
1231	missing resource (`404 not_found`). Migrating an execution to a missing
1232	version is likewise a missing resource, while migrating a completed or
1233	terminated execution is a conflict; a malformed migration body is a
1234	validation error, and a migration to the version already bound is a
1235	state-returning no-op rather than an error.
1236	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
1237	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
1238	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
1239	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
1240	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
1241	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
1242	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
1243	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
1244	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1245	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, more than ten attempts, a
1246	subscription declaring both `url` and `queue` or neither, an empty queue
1247	name, or a non-positive visibility timeout — is a
1248	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
1249	querying the delivery history or the queues of a missing execution is a
1250	missing resource. Declaring a queue name another workflow or execution of
1251	the same tenant already declared is a conflict. Pulling from or
1252	acknowledging a missing queue, and acknowledging an unknown or already
1253	acknowledged message, are missing resources; a pull body that is not an
1254	empty object, or an acknowledgement body without exactly an
1255	`idempotency_key` string, is a validation error. An approval
1256	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
1257	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
1258	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
1259	A decision by an approver who is
1260	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
1261	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
1262	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
1263	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
1264	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
1265	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
1266	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
1267	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
1268	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
1269	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
1270	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
1271	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
1272	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
1273	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
1274	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
1275	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
1276	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
1277	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
1278	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
1279	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
1280	
1281	## Tests
1282	
1283	```bash
1284	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
1285	```
1286	
1287
